subject: health
topic: Two hours a week in nature is linked to better health
angle: While spending at least 120 minutes a week in nature is linked to better health and well-being, the most effective nature-based interventions for mental health may occur in doses of 20 to 90 minutes.
title: The Dosage of Nature

hooks.text: How much nature do you actually need?
You think more nature is better. The data says otherwise.
You are missing the specific dosage of the outdoors.
Dust on a leaf. A heavy door. Twenty minutes of stillness.

reveal.headline: Nature benefits peak at specific doses.
reveal.body: While 120 minutes a week is linked to better health, the most effective interventions for mental health occur in doses of 20 to 90 minutes.

explain.headline: The limits of nature contact.
explain.body: Positive associations with health peak between 200-300 minutes per week. Beyond this point, there is no further gain.

matters.headline: The math of well-being.
matters.body: That may be why you do not need hours in the woods to see a change. Precise, shorter intervals may be the intended mechanism for mental relief.

example.headline: A walk to the corner.
example.body: You stand by the tree on your street for twenty minutes before entering your apartment building. The air is still. The leaves are heavy with dust. You breathe in once before the door clicks shut behind you.

stat.label: optimal dose for nature-based mental health interventions

claims.text: The most effective nature-based interventions were offered for between 8 and 12 weeks, and the optimal dose ranged from 20 to 90 min.
claims.quote: The most effective interventions were offered for between 8 and 12 weeks, and the optimal dose ranged from 20 to 90 min.

claims.text: Positive associations between nature contact and health peaked between 200-300 minutes per week with no further gain.
claims.quote: Positive associations peaked between 200-300 mins per week with no further gain.

claims.text: Residential greenness is linked to a statistically significant association with respiratory disease, low birth weight, cardiovascular disease, and other three diseases, except for allergic disease.
claims.quote: The meta-analysis result showed a statistically significant association between the residential greenness versus respiratory disease, low birth weight, cardiovascular disease, other three diseases, except for allergic disease.

claims.text: Spending at least 120 minutes a week in nature is linked to a significantly greater likelihood of reporting good health and high well-being compared to no nature contact.
claims.quote: Compared to no nature contact last week, the likelihood of reporting good health or high well-being became significantly greater with contact ≥120 mins (e. g. 120-179 mins: ORs [95%CIs]: Health = 1. 59 [1. 31-1. 92]; Well-being = 1. 23 [1. 08-1. 40]).

claims.text: Seven (78%) of the nine studies found a significant inverse relationship between an increase in surrounding greenness per 0·1 NDVI in a buffer zone of 500 m or less and the risk of all-cause mortality.

verdict: The evidence shows that regular nature contact and structured nature-based interventions are linked to improved mental and physical health outcomes, with specific benefits observed for disadvantaged groups.
caveat: The evidence for physical health improvements from nature-based interventions is less substantial than the evidence for mental health benefits.
caption:
Nature contact is linked to measurable improvements in physical and mental health. 

Research shows that structured interventions of 20 to 90 minutes are highly effective for mental health, though evidence for physical health improvements is less substantial. 

How many minutes do you spend outside today?
